View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost. 

They want you to help them! Will you?


-----Input-----

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

It's guaranteed that a_1 = 1, b_{n} = 0, a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_{n} and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_{n}.


-----Output-----

The only line of output must contain the minimum cost of cutting all the trees completely.

Please, do not write the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in С++. It is preferred to use the cin, cout streams or the %I64d specifier.


-----Examples-----

5 4 3 2 0

25

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost. 

They want you to help them! Will you?


-----Input-----

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

It's guaranteed that a_1 = 1, b_{n} = 0, a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_{n} and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_{n}.


-----Output-----

The only line of output must contain the minimum cost of cutting all the trees completely.

Please, do not write the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in С++. It is preferred to use the cin, cout streams or the %I64d specifier.


-----Examples-----

25

Problem

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost.

You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost. 

They want you to help them! Will you?


-----Input-----

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

It's guaranteed that a_1 = 1, b_{n} = 0, a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_{n} and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_{n}.


-----Output-----

The only line of output must contain the minimum cost of cutting all the trees completely.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money.

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost. 

They want you to help them! Will you?


-----Input-----

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

It's guaranteed that a_1 = 1, b_{n} = 0, a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_{n} and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_{n}.


-----Output-----

The only line of output must contain the minimum cost of cutting all the trees completely.

Please, do not write the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in С++. It is preferred to use the cin, cout streams or the %I64d specifier.

You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost. 

They want you to help them! Will you?


-----Input-----

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

It's guaranteed that a_1 = 1, b_{n} = 0, a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_{n} and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_{n}.


-----Output-----

The only line of output must contain the minimum cost of cutting all the trees completely.

Please, do not write the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in С++. It is preferred to use the cin, cout streams or the %I64d specifier.

I'll solve this step by step.

## Problem Understanding

1. We have n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_n
2. We can cut 1 unit from any tree at a time
3. When we cut, we need to recharge the chain saw
4. The cost of recharging depends on the maximum ID of trees that have been completely cut
5. If the maximum ID of completely cut trees is i, the cost is b_i
6. If no tree is completely cut, we can't recharge
7. We want to minimize the total cost to cut all trees completely

## Key Insights

1. Trees are ordered such that a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_n and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_n
2. The cost b_i decreases as i increases, so we want to use lower costs when possible
3. We can only cut trees that have been "activated" by being completely cut
4. To cut a tree of height h, we need to perform h cuts on it
5. After cutting a tree completely, it becomes available for recharging at cost b_i

## Strategy

Kalila and Dimna are two jackals living in a huge jungle. One day they decided to join a logging factory in order to make money. 

The manager of logging factory wants them to go to the jungle and cut n trees with heights a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n}. They bought a chain saw from a shop. Each time they use the chain saw on the tree number i, they can decrease the height of this tree by one unit. Each time that Kalila and Dimna use the chain saw, they need to recharge it. Cost of charging depends on the id of the trees which have been cut completely (a tree is cut completely if its height equal to 0). If the maximum id of a tree which has been cut completely is i (the tree that have height a_{i} in the beginning), then the cost of charging the chain saw would be b_{i}. If no tree is cut completely, Kalila and Dimna cannot charge the chain saw. The chainsaw is charged in the beginning. We know that for each i < j, a_{i} < a_{j} and b_{i} > b_{j} and also b_{n} = 0 and a_1 = 1. Kalila and Dimna want to cut all the trees completely, with minimum cost. 

They want you to help them! Will you?


-----Input-----

The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5). The second line of input contains n integers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{n} (1 ≤ a_{i} ≤ 10^9). The third line of input contains n integers b_1, b_2, ..., b_{n} (0 ≤ b_{i} ≤ 10^9).

It's guaranteed that a_1 = 1, b_{n} = 0, a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_{n} and b_1 > b_2 > ... > b_{n}.


-----Output-----

The only line of output must contain the minimum cost of cutting all the trees completely.

## Problem Understanding

We need to find the number of ways to climb a ladder of length `n` using jumps of up to `k` steps at a time.

This is a classic dynamic programming problem similar to the "climbing stairs" problem, but with the added constraint that we can jump up to `k` steps at a time.

## Step-by-Step Analysis

1. **Base Cases**:
   - If `n = 0`, there's exactly 1 way (stay at ground)
   - If `n = 1`, there's exactly 1 way (jump 1 step)

2. **Recurrence Relation**:
   - For position `i`, we can reach it from positions `i-1`, `i-2`, ..., `i-k`
   - So the number of ways to reach position `i` = sum of ways to reach all positions from `i-1` to `i-k`

3. **Example Walkthrough** (n=5, k=3):
   - Ways to reach position 0: 1
   - Ways to reach position 1: ways to reach position 0 = 1
   - Ways to reach position 2: ways to reach position 1 + ways to reach position 0 = 1 + 1 = 2
   - Ways to reach position 3: ways to reach position 2 + ways to reach position 1 + ways to reach position 0 = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4
   - Ways to reach position 4: ways to reach position 3 + ways to reach position 2 + ways to reach position 1 = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7
   - Ways to reach position 5: ways to reach position 4 + ways to reach position 3 + ways to reach position 2 = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13

This matches the example given (13 ways).

## Dynamic Programming Approach

We can use DP where `dp[i]` represents the number of ways to reach position `i`.

```python
dp[0] = 1  # base case: one way to stay at ground
for i in range(1, n+1):
    for j in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):  # jump of size j (1 to min(k,i))
        dp[i] += dp[i-j]
```

## Implementation

```python
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # Try all possible jumps from 1 to min(k, i)
    for jump in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):
        dp[i] += dp[i - jump]

print(dp[n])
```

## Problem Understanding

We need to find the number of ways to climb a ladder of length `n` using jumps of up to `k` steps. At each position, Bob can jump 1, 2, 3, ..., up to `k` steps.

This is a classic dynamic programming problem similar to the "climbing stairs" problem, but with a variable jump size limit.

## Approach

Let's define `dp[i]` as the number of ways to reach the i-th step of the ladder.

Base case:
- `dp[0] = 1` (one way to stay at ground level - do nothing)

For each step `i` from 1 to `n`:
- We can reach step `i` by jumping from step `i-1`, `i-2`, ..., `i-k` (but only if those positions are valid)
- So `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] + ... + dp[i-k]` (for valid indices)

## Step-by-step Example

For n=5, k=3:

- `dp[0] = 1` (base case)
- `dp[1] = dp[0] = 1` (can jump 1 step from 0)
- `dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1 + 1 = 2` (can jump 1 step from 1, or 2 steps from 0)
- `dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] + dp[0] = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4` (can jump 1, 2, or 3 steps)
- `dp[4] = dp[3] + dp[2] + dp[1] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7` (can jump 1, 2, or 3 steps)
- `dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] + dp[2] = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13`

This matches the expected answer of 13.

## Optimization

We can optimize the calculation by maintaining a sliding window sum to avoid recalculating the sum repeatedly.

## Implementation

```python
n = int(input())
k = int(input())

# dp[i] represents number of ways to reach step i
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = 1  # one way to stay at ground level

# Fill the dp array
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # Sum of ways from previous steps (i-1, i-2, ..., i-k)
    for j in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):
        dp[i] += dp[i - j]

print(dp[n])
```

## Problem Understanding

We need to find the number of ways to climb a ladder of length `n` where each jump can be of size 1, 2, 3, ..., up to `k` steps.

This is a classic dynamic programming problem similar to the "Climbing Stairs" problem, but with a constraint that each step can be at most `k` steps.

## Step-by-Step Analysis

1. **Base cases**:
   - If n = 0: There's exactly 1 way (don't move at all)
   - If n < 0: Impossible, so 0 ways
   - If n = 1: Only one way (jump 1 step)

2. **Recurrence relation**:
   - For a ladder of length n, we can reach it by jumping from position (n-1), (n-2), ..., (n-k)
   - So the number of ways to reach position n = sum of ways to reach positions (n-1), (n-2), ..., (n-k)

3. **Dynamic Programming approach**:
   - Let dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i
   - dp[0] = 1 (base case)
   - For each position i from 1 to n:
     - dp[i] = sum of dp[i-j] for all j from 1 to min(k, i)

## Example Verification

For n=5, k=3:

- dp[0] = 1
- dp[1] = dp[0] = 1
- dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1 + 1 = 2
- dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] + dp[0] = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4
- dp[4] = dp[3] + dp[2] + dp[1] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7
- dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] + dp[2] = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13

This matches the expected output of 13.

## Implementation

```python
n = int(input())
k = int(input())

# dp[i] represents number of ways to reach step i
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = 1  # One way to stay at ground

# Fill the dp array
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # Sum all ways from previous positions that can reach current position
    for j in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):
        dp[i] += dp[i - j]

print(dp[n])
```

The algorithm works as follows:
1. Initialize dp array with size n+1
2. Set dp[0] = 1 (base case)
3. For each step i from 1 to n, sum up all ways from steps i-1, i-2, ..., i-k (but not beyond 0)
4. Return dp[n]

Time complexity: O(n*k)
Space complexity: O(n)

## Step-by-Step Analysis

1. **Base cases:**
   - If `n = 0`: There's 1 way (don't move)
   - If `n < 0`: There are 0 ways (can't reach negative steps)

2. **Recurrence relation:**
   - To reach step `n`, Bob can jump from step `n-1`, `n-2`, ..., `n-k` (if those steps exist)
   - So the number of ways to reach step `n` = sum of ways to reach all previous steps from which he can jump

   - Let `dp[i]` = number of ways to reach step `i`
   - `dp[0] = 1` (one way to stay at ground)
   - For each step `i` from 1 to `n`:
     - `dp[i] = sum(dp[i-j])` for all `j` from 1 to `min(k, i)`

## Example walkthrough (n=5, k=3)

- `dp[0] = 1`

- `dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] + dp[2] = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13`

This matches the expected answer of 13.

```python
n = int(input())

print(dp[n])
```

## Problem Understanding

This is a classic dynamic programming problem similar to the "climbing stairs" problem, but with a twist - we can take up to `k` steps at a time.

Given:
- Ladder of length `n` (we need to reach the top)
- Each jump can be of size 1, 2, 3, ..., up to `k` steps
- We need to count the number of ways to reach the top

## Approach Analysis

This is a variation of the "number of ways to climb stairs" problem where instead of fixed step sizes (like only 1 or 2), we can take any step from 1 to k.

Let me think about the recurrence relation:
- To reach position `i`, we can come from positions `i-1`, `i-2`, ..., `i-k` (if those positions exist)
- So `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] + ... + dp[i-k]`

Base cases:
- `dp[0] = 1` (one way to stay at ground - do nothing)
- For positions beyond 0 and less than k, we need to build them up

## Step-by-step Solution

1. Create a DP array where `dp[i]` represents the number of ways to reach step `i`
2. Initialize `dp[0] = 1` (one way to be at the ground)
3. For each step from 1 to n, calculate the number of ways by summing up the ways from the previous k steps
4. Return `dp[n]`

Let me trace through the example:
- n = 5, k = 3
- dp[0] = 1
- dp[1] = dp[0] = 1 (can only come from step 0)
- dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1 + 1 = 2 (can come from step 1 or 0)
- dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] + dp[0] = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4
- dp[4] = dp[3] + dp[2] + dp[1] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7
- dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] + dp[2] = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13

This matches the expected output of 13.

## Edge Cases

- If n = 0, there's 1 way (don't move)
- If k >= n, we can use any step from 1 to n

## Implementation

```python
n = int(input())
k = int(input())

# dp[i] represents number of ways to reach step i
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = 1  # One way to stay at ground

# Fill the dp array
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # Sum the ways from the previous k steps
    for j in range(1, k + 1):
        if i - j >= 0:
            dp[i] += dp[i - j]

print(dp[n])
```

The algorithm works as follows:
1. Read n and k from input
2. Initialize dp array with size n+1
3. Set dp[0] = 1 (base case)
4. For each step i from 1 to n, add the number of ways to reach step (i-j) for all valid j (1 to k)
5. Print the result

Time Complexity: O(n*k)
Space Complexity: O(n)

## Problem Understanding

We need to find the number of ways to climb a ladder of length `n` using jumps of up to `k` steps. This is a classic dynamic programming problem similar to the "climbing stairs" problem, but with variable jump sizes.

## Step-by-Step Analysis

1. **Problem Type**: This is essentially a variant of the "number of ways to reach a step" problem where at each position, we can take 1, 2, ..., k steps.

2. **State Definition**: Let `dp[i]` = number of ways to reach step `i`.

3. **Base Cases**: 
   - `dp[0] = 1` (one way to stay at ground)
   - For any position `i`, we can reach it by jumping from any of the previous `min(i, k)` positions.

4. **Transition**: 
   - `dp[i] = sum(dp[i-j])` for all `j` from 1 to `min(i, k)`
   - This means we can reach step `i` by jumping from step `i-1`, `i-2`, ..., `i-k` (but only if those steps exist)

5. **Final Answer**: `dp[n]`

## Example Walkthrough

For n=5, k=3:
- We want to find ways to reach step 5 using jumps of 1, 2, or 3.

Let's calculate:
- `dp[0] = 1`
- `dp[1] = dp[0] = 1` (jump 1)
- `dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1 + 1 = 2` (jump 1+1 or jump 2)
- `dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] + dp[0] = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4` (jumps: 1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1, 3)
- `dp[4] = dp[3] + dp[2] + dp[1] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7` 
- `dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] + dp[2] = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13`

This matches the given example.

## Implementation

```python
n = int(input())
k = int(input())

# dp[i] represents number of ways to reach step i
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = 1  # One way to stay at ground (before any steps)

# Fill the dp array
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # Try all possible jump sizes from 1 to k
    for j in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):
        dp[i] += dp[i - j]

print(dp[n])
```

The algorithm works as follows:
1. Initialize `dp[0] = 1` (base case)
2. For each position `i` from 1 to `n`, calculate the number of ways by summing up all ways to reach positions `i-1`, `i-2`, ..., `i-k` (up to position `i`)
3. Return `dp[n]`

Time complexity: O(n*k)  
Space complexity: O(n)

Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Problem

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

In the rush of modern life, people often forget how beautiful the world is. The time to enjoy those around them is so little that some even stand in queues to several rooms at the same time in the clinic, running from one queue to another.

(Cultural note: standing in huge and disorganized queues for hours is a native tradition in Russia, dating back to the Soviet period. Queues can resemble crowds rather than lines. Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Now you're the last person in the queue till somebody else shows up. You keep an eye on the one who was last before you as he is your only chance to get to your destination) I'm sure many people have had the problem when a stranger asks who the last person in the queue is and even dares to hint that he will be the last in the queue and then bolts away to some unknown destination. These are the representatives of the modern world, in which the ratio of lack of time is so great that they do not even watch foreign top-rated TV series. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Having stood for about three hours in the queue, the Smart Beaver realized that many beavers had not seen who was supposed to stand in the queue before them and there was a huge mess. He came up to each beaver in the ECG room queue and asked who should be in front of him in the queue. If the beaver did not know his correct position in the queue, then it might be his turn to go get an ECG, or maybe he should wait for a long, long time...

As you've guessed, the Smart Beaver was in a hurry home, so he gave you all the necessary information for you to help him to determine what his number in the queue can be.

Input

The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 103) and x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) — the number of beavers that stand in the queue and the Smart Beaver's number, correspondingly. All willing to get to the doctor are numbered from 1 to n.

The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (0 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the number of the beaver followed by the i-th beaver. If ai = 0, then the i-th beaver doesn't know who is should be in front of him. It is guaranteed that values ai are correct. That is there is no cycles in the dependencies. And any beaver is followed by at most one beaver in the queue.

The input limits for scoring 30 points are (subproblem B1): 

  * It is guaranteed that the number of zero elements ai doesn't exceed 20. 



The input limits for scoring 100 points are (subproblems B1+B2): 

  * The number of zero elements ai is arbitrary. 

Output

Print all possible positions of the Smart Beaver in the line in the increasing order.

Examples

Input

6 1
2 0 4 0 6 0


Output

2
4
6


Input

6 2
2 3 0 5 6 0


Output

2
5


Input

4 1
0 0 0 0


Output

1
2
3
4


Input

6 2
0 0 1 0 4 5


Output

1
3
4
6

```python
# Build a mapping: for each beaver j, who follows j?
# We'll create a dict: follow[j] = the beaver that has j in front of it, or None

    # a[i] is the beaver in front of beaver (i+1)

    # if a[i] == j, then beaver (i+1) follows j
    if a[i] != 0:  # only if someone follows j

# Find roots: beavers j where no one has j in front of them

# Build chains from roots

for root in roots:
    chain = []
    current = root
    while True:
        chain.append(current)
        # Find next beaver that has current in front of it
        # i.e., find i such that a[i-1] == current
        # currently, current is in front of i
        # we want to find i such that a[i-1] == current
```

Steps:

1. Read input
2. Build chains from the predecessor relations (starting from ai=0)
3. For each chain, store the list of beavers and length
4. Find the chain that contains beaver x
5. For each possible start s from 1 to (n - length_of_chain + 1):
   a. Occupied positions: from s to s+length_of_chain-1
   b. Available positions: all positions 1 to n except those in [s, s+length-1]
   c. We need to check if we can partition the available positions into intervals that match the required lengths of the other chains

 So the algorithm is: 
1. Read n, x and array a of n integers
2. Build a mapping: for each value in 1 to n, the list of beavers that have that value as predecessor (ai = value for beaver i)
3. For each beaver with a[i-1] == 0 (i from 1 to n), it is a start, and we build the chain by following the mapping: from start, to the beaver with value = start, to the beaver with value = that value, and so on, until we reach a beaver not in the mapping (or the value not in the mapping)
4. For each chain, record the list of beavers in order (from start to end)
5. Find the chain that contains x, and its index i (0-indexed) in that chain
6. For each chain, get its length (number of beavers)
7. The other chains: all chains except this one, and their lengths
8. Generate all subset sums of the other chain lengths (using bit mask or iterative)
9. For each subset sum s, position = s + i + 1
10. Collect and output in increasing order.

You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

In the rush of modern life, people often forget how beautiful the world is. The time to enjoy those around them is so little that some even stand in queues to several rooms at the same time in the clinic, running from one queue to another.

(Cultural note: standing in huge and disorganized queues for hours is a native tradition in Russia, dating back to the Soviet period. Queues can resemble crowds rather than lines. Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Now you're the last person in the queue till somebody else shows up. You keep an eye on the one who was last before you as he is your only chance to get to your destination) I'm sure many people have had the problem when a stranger asks who the last person in the queue is and even dares to hint that he will be the last in the queue and then bolts away to some unknown destination. These are the representatives of the modern world, in which the ratio of lack of time is so great that they do not even watch foreign top-rated TV series. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Having stood for about three hours in the queue, the Smart Beaver realized that many beavers had not seen who was supposed to stand in the queue before them and there was a huge mess. He came up to each beaver in the ECG room queue and asked who should be in front of him in the queue. If the beaver did not know his correct position in the queue, then it might be his turn to go get an ECG, or maybe he should wait for a long, long time...

As you've guessed, the Smart Beaver was in a hurry home, so he gave you all the necessary information for you to help him to determine what his number in the queue can be.

Input

The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 103) and x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) — the number of beavers that stand in the queue and the Smart Beaver's number, correspondingly. All willing to get to the doctor are numbered from 1 to n.

The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (0 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the number of the beaver followed by the i-th beaver. If ai = 0, then the i-th beaver doesn't know who is should be in front of him. It is guaranteed that values ai are correct. That is there is no cycles in the dependencies. And any beaver is followed by at most one beaver in the queue.

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

In the rush of modern life, people often forget how beautiful the world is. The time to enjoy those around them is so little that some even stand in queues to several rooms at the same time in the clinic, running from one queue to another.

(Cultural note: standing in huge and disorganized queues for hours is a native tradition in Russia, dating back to the Soviet period. Queues can resemble crowds rather than lines. Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Now you're the last person in the queue till somebody else shows up. You keep an eye on the one who was last before you as he is your only chance to get to your destination) I'm sure many people have had the problem when a stranger asks who the last person in the queue is and even dares to hint that he will be the last in the queue and then bolts away to some unknown destination. These are the representatives of the modern world, in which the ratio of lack of time is so great that they do not even watch foreign top-rated TV series. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Having stood for about three hours in the queue, the Smart Beaver realized that many beavers had not seen who was supposed to stand in the queue before them and there was a huge mess. He came up to each beaver in the ECG room queue and asked who should be in front of him in the queue. If the beaver did not know his correct position in the queue, then it might be his turn to go get an ECG, or maybe he should wait for a long, long time...

As you've guessed, the Smart Beaver was in a hurry home, so he gave you all the necessary information for you to help him to determine what his number in the queue can be.

Input

The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 103) and x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) — the number of beavers that stand in the queue and the Smart Beaver's number, correspondingly. All willing to get to the doctor are numbered from 1 to n.

The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (0 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the number of the beaver followed by the i-th beaver. If ai = 0, then the i-th beaver doesn't know who is should be in front of him. It is guaranteed that values ai are correct. That is there is no cycles in the dependencies. And any beaver is followed by at most one beaver in the queue.

The input limits for scoring 30 points are (subproblem B1): 

  * It is guaranteed that the number of zero elements ai doesn't exceed 20. 



The input limits for scoring 100 points are (subproblems B1+B2): 

  * The number of zero elements ai is arbitrary. 

Output

Print all possible positions of the Smart Beaver in the line in the increasing order.

```
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Find all roots (beavers with ai = 0)
roots = []

    if a[i] == 0:
        roots.append(i)  # index i, beaver i+1

positions = []

# For each root, build chain and find position of x
for root_idx in roots:
    # Start with beaver root_idx + 1
    current_beaver = root_idx + 1
    chain = []
    # We need to follow the chain until we hit a beaver that has no one following it
    # But we only follow from a[i] for current beaver
    # a[j] is the beaver that beaver j+1 follows
    # So for beaver current_beaver, it follows a[current_beaver-1]
    # But we are at current_beaver, and we want to follow from current_beaver to next
    # Actually, the chain is: root -> next -> next
    # For beaver number b, it follows a[b-1]
    # So next beaver is a[b-1]
    # We can build the chain until we reach a beaver that has no one following it (a[beaver-1] = 0 or not in the chain)
    # We don't need to build the whole chain, only until we reach x or find a loop
    # But the problem says no cycles
    
    # Build the chain by following the follow relationship
    chain = []
    current = current_beaver
    while current <= n:
        chain.append(current)
        # The next beaver is a[current-1] if a[current-1] > 0 and a[current-1] <= n
        # But a[current-1] is the beaver that current follows, so the next in chain is a[current-1]
        # Only if a[current-1] > 0 and a[current-1] is a valid beaver number (1 to n)
        next_beaver = a[current-1] if current <= n else 0
        if next_beaver == 0:
            break
        current = next_beaver
        # We only go if next_beaver is not 0 and within bounds
        if next_beaver > n or next_beaver < 1:
            break
    
    # In this chain, find the position of x
    # chain has beavers in order: first is root, then the one it follows, etc.
    # position is index+1
    for idx, beaver in enumerate(chain):
        if beaver == x:
            positions.append(idx + 1)
            break

# Output all positions in increasing order (they should be in order from construction)
positions.sort()
for pos in positions:
    print(pos)
```

```
n, x = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Build a dictionary: pred[beaver] = the beaver that is in front of it
# a[i] is the beaver in front of beaver (i+1)
pred = {}
for i in range(n):
    if a[i] > 0:  # if there is a predecessor
        pred[i+1] = a[i]

# Find all roots: beavers that have no predecessor
roots = []
for i in range(1, n+1):
    if i not in pred:
        roots.append(i)

positions = []

# For each root, build the chain in order
 for root in roots:
    chain = []
    current = root
    while current in pred:
        chain.append(current)
        current = pred[current]
    # After the loop, current is not in pred, so we add it
    chain.append(current)
    # In this chain, find the position of x
    for idx, beaver in enumerate(chain):
        if beaver == x:
            positions.append(idx+1)
            break

# Output in increasing order (should be sorted)
positions.sort()
for pos in positions:
    print(pos)
```

You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

In the rush of modern life, people often forget how beautiful the world is. The time to enjoy those around them is so little that some even stand in queues to several rooms at the same time in the clinic, running from one queue to another.

(Cultural note: standing in huge and disorganized queues for hours is a native tradition in Russia, dating back to the Soviet period. Queues can resemble crowds rather than lines. Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Now you're the last person in the queue till somebody else shows up. You keep an eye on the one who was last before you as he is your only chance to get to your destination) I'm sure many people have had the problem when a stranger asks who the last person in the queue is and even dares to hint that he will be the last in the queue and then bolts away to some unknown destination. These are the representatives of the modern world, in which the ratio of lack of time is so great that they do not even watch foreign top-rated TV series. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Having stood for about three hours in the queue, the Smart Beaver realized that many beavers had not seen who was supposed to stand in the queue before them and there was a huge mess. He came up to each beaver in the ECG room queue and asked who should be in front of him in the queue. If the beaver did not know his correct position in the queue, then it might be his turn to go get an ECG, or maybe he should wait for a long, long time...

As you've guessed, the Smart Beaver was in a hurry home, so he gave you all the necessary information for you to help him to determine what his number in the queue can be.

Input

The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 103) and x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) — the number of beavers that stand in the queue and the Smart Beaver's number, correspondingly. All willing to get to the doctor are numbered from 1 to n.

The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (0 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the number of the beaver followed by the i-th beaver. If ai = 0, then the i-th beaver doesn't know who is should be in front of him. It is guaranteed that values ai are correct. That is there is no cycles in the dependencies. And any beaver is followed by at most one beaver in the queue.

The input limits for scoring 30 points are (subproblem B1):

The input limits for scoring 100 points are (subproblems B1+B2): 

  * The number of zero elements ai is arbitrary. 

Output

Print all possible positions of the Smart Beaver in the line in the increasing order.

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

In the rush of modern life, people often forget how beautiful the world is. The time to enjoy those around them is so little that some even stand in queues to several rooms at the same time in the clinic, running from one queue to another.

(Cultural note: standing in huge and disorganized queues for hours is a native tradition in Russia, dating back to the Soviet period. Queues can resemble crowds rather than lines. Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Now you're the last person in the queue till somebody else shows up. You keep an eye on the one who was last before you as he is your only chance to get to your destination) I'm sure many people have had the problem when a stranger asks who the last person in the queue is and even dares to hint that he will be the last in the queue and then bolts away to some unknown destination. These are the representatives of the modern world, in which the ratio of lack of time is so great that they do not even watch foreign top-rated TV series. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Having stood for about three hours in the queue, the Smart Beaver realized that many beavers had not seen who was supposed to stand in the queue before them and there was a huge mess. He came up to each beaver in the ECG room queue and asked who should be in front of him in the queue. If the beaver did not know his correct position in the queue, then it might be his turn to go get an ECG, or maybe he should wait for a long, long time...

As you've guessed, the Smart Beaver was in a hurry home, so he gave you all the necessary information for you to help him to determine what his number in the queue can be.

Input

The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 103) and x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) — the number of beavers that stand in the queue and the Smart Beaver's number, correspondingly. All willing to get to the doctor are numbered from 1 to n.

The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (0 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the number of the beaver followed by the i-th beaver. If ai = 0, then the i-th beaver doesn't know who is should be in front of him. It is guaranteed that values ai are correct. That is there is no cycles in the dependencies. And any beaver is followed by at most one beaver in the queue.

The input limits for scoring 30 points are (subproblem B1): 

  * It is guaranteed that the number of zero elements ai doesn't exceed 20. 



The input limits for scoring 100 points are (subproblems B1+B2): 

  * The number of zero elements ai is arbitrary. 

Output

Print all possible positions of the Smart Beaver in the line in the increasing order.

Examples

6 1
2 0 4 0 6 0

6

2
5

0 0 0 0

4

So algorithm:

1. Build all chains from the input
2. Find the chain containing the smart beaver x
3. Let chain_length = L, and position_in_chain = p (0-indexed)
4. Let other_chains = list of (length) for all other chains

   a. left1 = s - 1  # positions 1 to s-1
   b. left2 = n - s - L + 1  # positions s+L to n
   c. If left1 < 0 or left2 < 0, skip (should not happen)
   d. Check if other_chains can be packed into segments of length left1 and left2.
      - This is done with DP: dp[j] = whether we can achieve sum j in segment1 for the other chains
      - Initially dp[0] = True
      - For each chain of length l in other_chains:
          new_dp = copy of dp
          for each j in dp:
             if j + l <= left1: new_dp[j+l] = True
             if (total_sum - j) + l <= left2: new_dp[j] = True  # but we need to know total_sum
      - We need to know the total sum of other_chains = total_other = sum(other_chains)
      - total_other should equal left1 + left2 = n - L
      - So if total_other != n - L, skip (should not happen)
   e. If the packing is possible, then the position of x is s + p
   f. Add s + p to the answer set

7. Output the answer set in increasing order.

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

In the rush of modern life, people often forget how beautiful the world is. The time to enjoy those around them is so little that some even stand in queues to several rooms at the same time in the clinic, running from one queue to another.

(Cultural note: standing in huge and disorganized queues for hours is a native tradition in Russia, dating back to the Soviet period. Queues can resemble crowds rather than lines. Not to get lost in such a queue, a person should follow a strict survival technique: you approach the queue and ask who the last person is, somebody answers and you join the crowd. Now you're the last person in the queue till somebody else shows up. You keep an eye on the one who was last before you as he is your only chance to get to your destination) I'm sure many people have had the problem when a stranger asks who the last person in the queue is and even dares to hint that he will be the last in the queue and then bolts away to some unknown destination. These are the representatives of the modern world, in which the ratio of lack of time is so great that they do not even watch foreign top-rated TV series. Such people often create problems in queues, because the newcomer does not see the last person in the queue and takes a place after the "virtual" link in this chain, wondering where this legendary figure has left.

The Smart Beaver has been ill and he's made an appointment with a therapist. The doctor told the Beaver the sad news in a nutshell: it is necessary to do an electrocardiogram. The next day the Smart Beaver got up early, put on the famous TV series on download (three hours till the download's complete), clenched his teeth and bravely went to join a queue to the electrocardiogram room, which is notorious for the biggest queues at the clinic.

Having stood for about three hours in the queue, the Smart Beaver realized that many beavers had not seen who was supposed to stand in the queue before them and there was a huge mess. He came up to each beaver in the ECG room queue and asked who should be in front of him in the queue. If the beaver did not know his correct position in the queue, then it might be his turn to go get an ECG, or maybe he should wait for a long, long time...

As you've guessed, the Smart Beaver was in a hurry home, so he gave you all the necessary information for you to help him to determine what his number in the queue can be.

Input

The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 103) and x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) — the number of beavers that stand in the queue and the Smart Beaver's number, correspondingly. All willing to get to the doctor are numbered from 1 to n.

The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (0 ≤ ai ≤ n) — the number of the beaver followed by the i-th beaver. If ai = 0, then the i-th beaver doesn't know who is should be in front of him. It is guaranteed that values ai are correct. That is there is no cycles in the dependencies. And any beaver is followed by at most one beaver in the queue.

The input limits for scoring 30 points are (subproblem B1): 

  * It is guaranteed that the number of zero elements ai doesn't exceed 20. 



The input limits for scoring 100 points are (subproblems B1+B2): 

  * The number of zero elements ai is arbitrary. 

Output

Print all possible positions of the Smart Beaver in the line in the increasing order.

## Problem Understanding

1. We have a queue of n beavers numbered 1 to n
2. Each beaver i knows who is in front of them (a_i), or 0 if they don't know
3. The "last person" in the queue is the one who has no one behind them (a_i = 0)
4. We need to find all possible positions (numbers) that the Smart Beaver (number x) can have in the queue

## Key Insights

1. The queue forms a directed graph where each beaver points to the beaver in front of them (or 0 if unknown)
2. Since there are no cycles and each beaver is followed by at most one other, this forms a forest of trees where each "chain" goes from someone to someone else
3. The "last" people in each chain are those who have no one behind them (a_i = 0)
4. For each chain, the beavers form a sequence where each beaver points to the one in front of them
5. If a beaver doesn't know who's in front of them (a_i = 0), they could be at any position in their chain

- If a beaver doesn't know who's in front of them (a_i = 0), they could be at the beginning of a chain (position 1) or somewhere else in the chain

```python
        base = base * base % mod
```

We need to find the number of ways to choose k lamps such that there exists a moment when all k lamps are turned on simultaneously.

For k lamps to be on at the same time, there must exist a time t such that:

```python
import sys
import bisect

MOD = 998244353

def precompute_factorials(n):
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
    inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv_fact[n] = pow(fact[n], MOD-2, MOD)
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD
    return fact, inv_fact

def nCr(n, r, fact, inv_fact):
    if r < 0 or r > n:
        return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD * inv_fact[n-r] % MOD
```

But there is a flaw: in the representative list, we are using the value of r from the last occurrence in the sorted array, and we are grouping by l.

However, when we iterate over the representatives, we are only including one per distinct l.

But in the sorted array, we might have multiple lamps with the same l, and we are only taking the last one in the sorted array.

This is correct.

Let's fix the code.

We need to store for each distinct l, the r value of the last occurrence in the sorted array.

We can do that in one pass.

Final implementation:

```python
import sys
import bisect

MOD = 998244353

def precompute_factorials(n):
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
    inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv_fact[n] = pow(fact[n], MOD-2, MOD)
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD
    return fact, inv_fact

def nCr(n, r, fact, inv_fact):
```

```python
import sys
import bisect

MOD = 998244353

def precompute_factorials(n):
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
    inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv_fact[n] = pow(fact[n], MOD-2, MOD)
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD
    return fact, inv_fact

def nCr(n, r, fact, inv_fact):
    if r < 0 or r > n:
        return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD * inv_fact[n-r] % MOD

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    
    n = int(data[0])
    k = int(data[1])
    
    lamps = []
    index = 2

        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by l_i

    # Group by l_i and take the last occurrence (highest index in the sorted array for that l)
    last_r = {}
    for l, r in lamps:
        last_r[l] = r  # store the r value for the last occurrence of l in the sorted array
    
    # Create list of representatives with (l, r) for each distinct l, and sort by l
    representatives = []
    for l in last_r:
        representatives.append((l, last_r[l]))
    representatives.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials up to n
    fact, inv_fact = precompute_factorials(n)
    
    # Maintain a sorted list of r values (for lamps with l_i < current l)
    r_list = []
    
    total = 0
    for l, r in representatives:
        # Count number of values in r_list that are >= l
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(r_list, l)
        count = len(r_list) - pos
        if count >= k-1:
            total = (total + nCr(count, k-1, fact, inv_fact)) % MOD
        # Add the current r to r_list
        bisect.insort(r_list, r)
    
    print(total)

if __name__ == "__main__":
```

```python
        bisect.insort(right_list, r)
    
    print(total % MOD)

# Implementation:

MOD = 998244353

def solve():
    import bisect
    
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by left endpoint
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n
    max_n = n
    fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    for i in range(1, max_n + 1):
        fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD
    
    def mod_inverse(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    inv_fact[max_n] = mod_inverse(fact[max_n], MOD)
    for i in range(max_n - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = (inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD
    
    def ncr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return (fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD) * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Maintain a sorted list of right endpoints
    right_list = []
    total = 0
    
    for l, r in lamps:
        # Find the first position where element >= l
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(right_list, l)
        count_S_prime = len(right_list) - pos  # number of right endpoints >= l in lamps with left < current l
        
        count_S = count_S_prime + 1  # including current lamp
        
        # Add combination count
        if count_S >= k:
            add_val = (ncr(count_S, k) - ncr(count_S_prime, k)) % MOD
            total = (total + add_val) % MOD
        else:
            add_val = 0
        
        # Insert current right endpoint
        bisect.insort(right_list, r)
    
    print(total % MOD)

solve()
```

# Implementation:

MOD = 998244353

def solve():
    import bisect
    
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by left endpoint
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n
    max_n = n
    fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    for i in range(1, max_n + 1):
        fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD
    
    def mod_inverse(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    inv_fact[max_n] = mod_inverse(fact[max_n], MOD)
    for i in range(max_n - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = (inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD
    
    def ncr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return (fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD) * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Maintain a sorted list of right endpoints
    right_list = []
    total = 0
    
    for l, r in lamps:
        # Find the first position where element >= l
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(right_list, l)
        count_S_prime = len(right_list) - pos  # number of right endpoints >= l in lamps with left < current l
        
        count_S = count_S_prime + 1  # including current lamp
        
        # Add combination count
        if count_S >= k:
            add_val = (ncr(count_S, k) - ncr(count_S_prime, k)) % MOD
            total = (total + add_val) % MOD
        else:
            add_val = 0
        
        # Insert current right endpoint
        bisect.insort(right_list, r)
    
    print(total % MOD)

solve()

```python
def solve():
    MOD = 998244353
    
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by left endpoint
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials
    max_n = n
    fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    for i in range(1, max_n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
    
    def mod_inverse(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    inv_fact[max_n] = mod_inverse(fact[max_n], MOD)
    for i in range(max_n - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i + 1] * (i + 1) % MOD
    
    def nCr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Sort by left endpoint
    lamps.sort()
    
    # We'll maintain a sorted list of right endpoints of lamps processed so far
    # For each lamp i, we want to count how many processed lamps have right >= lamps[i][0]
    # We process lamps in order of increasing left endpoint
    import bisect
    
    # Keep a sorted list of right endpoints
    right_endpoints = []
    total_ways = 0
    
    for i in range(n):
        l_i, r_i = lamps[i]
        
        # Add current lamp's right endpoint to the list
        # We'll insert it in sorted order
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(right_endpoints, r_i)
        right_endpoints.insert(pos, r_i)
        
        # Count how many lamps have right >= l_i
        # Since we want right >= l_i, we find the first position where right >= l_i
        pos_ge = bisect.bisect_left(right_endpoints, l_i)
        count_ge = len(right_endpoints) - pos_ge
        
        # We need to choose k-1 lamps from these count_ge lamps
        # This gives one valid combination where the maximum left endpoint is l_i
        if count_ge >= k - 1:
            total_ways = (total_ways + nCr(count_ge, k - 1)) % MOD
    
    print(total_ways)

solve()
```

```python
def solve():
    MOD = 998244353
    
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by left endpoint
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials
    max_n = n
    fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    for i in range(1, max_n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
    
    def mod_inverse(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    inv_fact[max_n] = mod_inverse(fact[max_n], MOD)
    for i in range(max_n - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i + 1] * (i + 1) % MOD
    
    def nCr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Sort by left endpoint
    lamps.sort()
    
    # We'll maintain a sorted list of right endpoints of lamps processed so far
    # For each lamp i, we want to count how many processed lamps have right >= lamps[i][0]
    # We process lamps in order of increasing left endpoint
    import bisect
    
    # Keep a sorted list of right endpoints
    right_endpoints = []
    total_ways = 0
    
    for i in range(n):
        l_i, r_i = lamps[i]
        
        # Count how many processed lamps have right >= l_i
        # Since we want right >= l_i, we find the first position where right >= l_i
        pos_ge = bisect.bisect_left(right_endpoints, l_i)
        count_ge = len(right_endpoints) - pos_ge
        
        # We need to choose k-1 lamps from these count_ge lamps
        if count_ge >= k - 1:
            total_ways = (total_ways + nCr(count_ge, k - 1)) % MOD
        
        # Add current lamp's right endpoint to the list
        # We insert in sorted order
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(right_endpoints, r_i)
        right_endpoints.insert(pos, r_i)
    
    print(total_ways)

solve()
```

```python
import bisect
from collections import defaultdict

MOD = 998244353

def solve():
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by starting time
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials
    max_val = n + 10
    fact = [1] * (max_val + 1)
    for i in range(1, max_val + 1):
        fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD
    
    def mod_inv(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (max_val + 1)
    inv_fact[max_val] = mod_inv(fact[max_val], MOD)
    for i in range(max_val - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = (inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD
    
    def nCr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return (fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD) * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Maintain sorted list of r values
    r_list = []
    ans = 0
    
    for l, r in lamps:
        # Query number of elements >= l in r_list
        # r_list contains r values for lamps processed so far
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(r_list, l)
        count_greater = len(r_list) - idx
```

```python
import bisect

MOD = 998244353

def solve():
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by starting time
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials for combinations
    # We need combinations up to n
    max_n = n
    fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    for i in range(1, max_n + 1):
        fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD
    
    def mod_inv(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (max_n + 1)
    inv_fact[max_n] = mod_inv(fact[max_n], MOD)
    for i in range(max_n - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = (inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD
    
    def nCr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return (fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD) * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Maintain sorted list of r values from previous lamps
    r_list = []
    ans = 0
    
    for l, r in lamps:
        # Count number of j < i with r_j >= l
        # In sorted list r_list, find first index >= l
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(r_list, l)
        count = len(r_list) - idx
        
        # We need to choose k-1 lamps from these 'count' lamps
        if count >= k - 1:
            ans = (ans + nCr(count, k - 1)) % MOD
        
        # Add current r to r_list
        bisect.insort(r_list, r)
    
    print(ans)

solve()
```

View Problem Statement 
You are an expert Python programmer. You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests.

Solve the following coding problem using the programming language python:

Ori and Sein have overcome many difficult challenges. They finally lit the Shrouded Lantern and found Gumon Seal, the key to the Forlorn Ruins. When they tried to open the door to the ruins... nothing happened.

Ori was very surprised, but Sein gave the explanation quickly: clever Gumon decided to make an additional defence for the door.

There are n lamps with Spirit Tree's light. Sein knows the time of turning on and off for the i-th lamp — l_i and r_i respectively. To open the door you have to choose k lamps in such a way that there will be a moment of time when they all will be turned on.

While Sein decides which of the k lamps to pick, Ori is interested: how many ways there are to pick such k lamps that the door will open? It may happen that Sein may be wrong and there are no such k lamps. The answer might be large, so print it modulo 998 244 353.

Input

First line contains two integers n and k (1 ≤ n ≤ 3 ⋅ 10^5, 1 ≤ k ≤ n) — total number of lamps and the number of lamps that must be turned on simultaneously.

## Problem Understanding

We need to find the number of ways to choose k lamps such that there exists a moment when all k lamps are turned on simultaneously.

For k lamps to be on simultaneously, there must be some time t such that t is in the intersection of all k lamps' intervals.

For two intervals [l_i, r_i] and [l_j, r_j], their intersection is [max(l_i, l_j), min(r_i, r_j)] and this intersection is non-empty if and only if max(l_i, l_j) ≤ min(r_i, r_j).

## Key Insight

For a set of k lamps to have a common time when all are on, we need to find all combinations of k lamps where the intersection of their intervals is non-empty.

A crucial observation: if we sort the lamps by their start time, then for any valid combination, the intersection will be from max(start times) to min(end times).

So we can:
1. Sort lamps by their start time
2. For each possible value of max(start time), check if there are enough lamps that end after this max start time

Now I need to implement:
- Binary search to count end times ≥ l_i
- Precompute binomial coefficients up to n (since k ≤ n)
- Use bisect module

```python
import bisect

MOD = 998244353

def solve():
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by start time
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD
    
    def mod_inverse(a, mod):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv_fact[n] = mod_inverse(fact[n], MOD)
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = (inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD
    
    def nCr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return (fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD) * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Create a list of end times and maintain it in sorted order
    end_times = []
    total_ans = 0
    
    for l, r in lamps:
        # Insert r into end_times (maintain sorted order)
        bisect.insort(end_times, r)
        
        # Count how many end times are >= l
        # end_times is sorted in increasing order, so we need to find the first position where value >= l
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(end_times, l)
        c = len(end_times) - pos  # number of elements >= l
        
        # Number of ways to choose k-1 lamps from the c-1 lamps (excluding the current lamp)
        # We must have at least k lamps available
        ways = nCr(c - 1, k - 1)
        total_ans = (total_ans + ways) % MOD
    
    print(total_ans)

solve()
```

```python
import bisect

MOD = 998244353

def solve():
    n, k = map(int, input().split())
    lamps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        l, r = map(int, input().split())
        lamps.append((l, r))
    
    # Sort by start time
    lamps.sort()
    
    # Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD
    
    def mod_inverse(a, mod=MOD):
        return pow(a, mod - 2, mod)
    
    inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv_fact[n] = mod_inverse(fact[n])
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = (inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD
    
    def nCr(n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return (fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD) * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
    
    # Create a list of end times and maintain it in sorted order
    end_times = []
    total_ans = 0
    
    for l, r in lamps:
        # Insert r into end_times (maintain sorted order)
        bisect.insort(end_times, r)
        
        # Count how many end times are >= l
        # end_times is sorted in increasing order, so we need to find the first position where value >= l
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(end_times, l)
        c = len(end_times) - pos  # number of elements >= l
        
        # Number of ways to choose k-1 lamps from the c-1 lamps (excluding the current lamp)
        # We must have at least k lamps available
        ways = nCr(c - 1, k - 1)
        total_ans = (total_ans + ways) % MOD
    
    print(total_ans)

solve()
```

This should be correct. I'll submit this. 

Note: The end_times list will contain end times from all lamps processed so far, and we count how many have end_time >= current l_i. Then we add C(c-1, k-1) where c is that count. This counts the number of ways to choose k lamps with maximum start time at current l_i (by fixing this lamp and choosing k-1 from the c-1 other candidates that satisfy the condition).

And since each valid set has a unique maximum start time, we don't overcount.

The complexity is O(n log n) due to sorting and insertion, and O(n) for the binomial coefficients with precomputation.
